item.title: Claude solves two open problems in the physics of black holes
item.abstract: 01 Introduction Claude has solved two open problems in theoretical physics. Both concern black holes and the search for a theory of quantum gravity. In the first, it completed a calculation that physicists set up more than 20 years ago, but which had never been solved. Claude’s result showed that a sudden transition associated with the formation of black holes persists even where spacetime no longer has a definite shape. In the second, Claude found the exact limit of the simplest version of a technique used to test candidate theories of quantum gravity. This post explains both findings, first in plain terms and then in more technical detail. The preprints are available here and here . Introduction Modern physics rests on two frameworks: general relativity and quantum mechanics. General relativity describes very large things, like stars; quantum mechanics describes very small things, such as atoms. Both are astonishingly good at predicting how the universe behaves, but they’re mathematically incompatible. Finding a theory that unites them—“quantum gravity”—is one of the field’s biggest goals. Black holes are a natural testing ground, because they’re one of the few areas where both relativity and quantum mechanics matter—they pack immense mass into a very small space. One of the most useful tools for studying quantum gravity is called holographic duality . The real universe has three dimensions of space and one of time, which relativity combines into four-dimensional spacetime. But physicists studying quantum gravity often work with simpler model universes that they can understand in more detail. The basic idea of holographic duality is that some of these theoretical universes can be described in two ways: as a complete universe with gravity and spacetime, and in quantum terms, with no gravity at all, “written” on the universe’s outer boundary. Just as a real hologram encodes a 3D image on a 2D plane, the quantum model encodes all the information of the universe in one dimension fewer (a universe with four dimensions of space, for instance, can be fully described by a quantum theory with three). This lets physicists turn hard questions about gravity into questions about quantum physics, which are sometimes easier to answer. The first problem Claude solved concerns what happens when you heat up one of these theoretical universes. At low temperatures, the universe fills up with a gas of particles. Above a certain temperature, a black hole forms instead. In 1983, Stephen Hawking and Don Page showed that this switch is abrupt: it’s a phase transition, similar to how water suddenly boils at 100°C. But Hawking and Page’s calculation relies on general relativity, which holds only when the universe is vast, compared with the tiny scale at which that description breaks down. As the theoretical universe shrinks toward that smaller scale, spacetime loses any definite shape and becomes blurry, and nobody knows how to do the calculation on the gravity side of the duality. On the quantum side, though, the same situation can be calculated, at least in principle. In 1999, physicists found that there was a phase transition in that regime as well. But they didn’t know whether it was abrupt, like Hawking and Page’s, or smooth. In 2003, a group of physicists set out the calculation that would settle the question , but it was extremely complex and was never completed. Claude did it by running a small research group of copies of itself, in which it worked out almost every piece of the calculation independently and checked its math against known results. It showed that the phase transition is abrupt. The same sudden switch appears at both extremes, suggesting that black hole formation isn’t just a feature of relativity but is actually built into the underlying quantum theory. The second problem concerns a simplified theoretical universe with two dimensions of space instead of three. This universe is straightforward enough to study in detail, but still has black holes and other mysteries similar to those of our own universe. Even in this simpler universe, physicists don’t know how to create a full theory of quantum gravity, so they approach it from the other direction: rather than building a single, correct theory, they try to rule out wrong ones by showing that they are internally inconsistent. This method is called bootstrapping . Since 2009, physicists have used a version of this method to set a ceiling on how heavy the lightest black hole in such a universe could be. Any theory that breaks the ceiling is ruled out, and each lowering of the ceiling narrows the search. Results from numerical calculations hinted at where the best possible ceiling lay, but they couldn’t prove it, and the best proven ceiling was well short of what the numerical results suggested. Claude Fable 5.2 noticed a pattern in the numerical results that physicists had missed and borrowed a method from elsewhere in math and physics to calculate the precise ceiling for the simplest version of this technique and prove that it could not be lowered. It doesn’t identify the correct theory, but it may point physicists in the right direction. Neither result describes our own universe directly, and neither has practical applications, but both contribute to a long-running theoretical effort to understand how quantum mechanics and relativity fit together. In the rest of this post, we explain in more detail what each problem was and what Claude did to solve them. A note about Claude’s methods In August, an Anthropic researcher, Hongbin Chen, was testing Claude’s capabilities as a side project. He asked Claude to draw up a list of interesting open problems in theoretical physics, specifically focusing on black holes and the bootstrap method. Claude came back hours later with 22 candidates, and Hongbin set up separate agents to work on each one; they could read each other’s progress posts and collaborate when working on related problems. The agents ran in the background, with no special setup, for about six weeks. The agents solved the two problems in this post. One was the Hawking-Page phase transition, the question of when a hot gas turns into a black hole. Weeks after one of the agents reached a solution, a physicist, who had independently used Claude to tackle the same problem, shared his result, and a colleague realized that Hongbin’s agent had reached the same answer earlier. The two solutions used different methods, so they were a useful check on each other. The modular bootstrap result came from several agents. The one that was assigned the problem spotted the pattern in the numerical results when surveying the bootstrap literature, and another one—which was working on a mathematically related problem about how tightly spheres can be packed into a high-dimensional space—turned that pattern into a method. It found that this method reproduced a sphere-packing result recently proved by an OpenAI model . Claude then applied the same method to the bootstrap problem, which an earlier Claude agent had tried, and failed, to solve in 61 parallel attempts. Two other agents also independently arrived at the same answer. One half of the final proof, showing that the ceiling can’t be lowered, follows the strategy of the OpenAI proof. In September, the results were formally verified in Lean, a computerized proof checker. Claude then wrote the paper with minimal guidance, and a physicist checked every main result. The Hawking-Page transition To understand the first problem, we need to start with something much more familiar: a walk through New York City. Two equally good routes from Penn Station (A) to the High Line entrance (B). In theory, a quantum particle can take both simultaneously. Imagine that you’re heading from Penn Station to the High Line entrance on West 30th Street and 10th Avenue, and there are two equally good routes.

item.title: Co-Designing Sparse Attention for Efficient Long-Context Inference
item.abstract: Agentic workloads, long documents, and large codebases are pushing context lengths from tens of thousands of tokens to hundreds of thousands. At those lengths, attention becomes the most expensive part of a transformer layer. Dense attention scores every query against every key, so its cost per query grows with the context length N, and at 128K tokens it can take most of the prefill time in a layer. The model-level solution is sparse attention, a transformer technique in which each query attends to only a small subset of the context, chosen per query, instead of all of it. This cuts both the compute and the memory traffic of attention on long context. This post is a practical primer for model developers designing sparse attention that runs well on NVIDIA GPUs. It focuses on model-level sparse attention, where sparsity is trained into the model, rather than drop-in methods applied after training such as BLASST , MInference , or Quest . A production FP8 kernel is used to sweep the indexer’s design knobs (query heads, key heads, head dimension, compression ratio, and speculative-decoding depth), measure how Top-k cost scales, and compare token-level with block-level core attention. Each section explains what the hardware rewards and why, and ends with a guideline you can apply to your own design. This post follows the same co-design approach as the earlier posts on dense attention and hardware-friendly LLM design . What is sparse attention and why does it matter? Sparse attention is an AI optimization technique that limits which prior tokens each query attends to. Instead of attending to the entire context, each query attends to only the \(k\) most relevant keys, typically a few thousand. Core attention then stops scaling with context. But those \(k\) keys have to be found, and the component that finds them, the indexer, still scores all \(N\) keys. The cost does not disappear; it moves into the indexer. DeepSeek-R1 (dense MLA) versus DeepSeek V3.2 (DSA) Sparse attention has three stages (Figure 2). An indexer scores every key, Top-k keeps the \(k\) highest scores, and core attention runs softmax attention over those \(k\) keys and values. The last two stages scale with \(k\), the indexer with \(N\). Figure 2. The three stages of sparse attention The indexer design space An indexer is a small attention-like block. Query heads score the current query against a cache of indexer keys, and post-processing operations (such as a ReLU and weighted sum) turn the scores into one logit per key. item.title: Mathematical proof, powered by AI. And no hallucinations!
item.abstract: Every day brings new evidence of the awesome power of AI. There have been dramatic developments in mathematics: AI models are solving tough problems from Mathematical Olympiads and even some big open research problems. But AI agents are notorious for simply making stuff up, or “hallucinating”: don’t we have to check their solutions carefully? In fact, the computer can check the agent’s proofs for us, and better still, proof checking can be interleaved with proof generation, keeping it on the right track. To be checked, the proof must be written in some logical formalism: a precise language that expresses mathematical reasoning. Proof assistants are apps designed for writing and checking formal proofs. They include Lean, favored by many mathematicians; HOL Light, used at AWS to formally verify high-performance cryptographic code (including for post-quantum cryptography); and Isabelle, used at AWS to verify the Nitro Isolation Engine. They were originally built to help human users write proofs, but now the “user” will be an AI agent. Most proof assistants are suitable for this task. In this post, we’ll focus on Isabelle. To generate formal proofs, we need a way for the AI agent and the proof assistant to talk to each other. Fortunately, we have the Model Context Protocol (MCP), which is supported by all the leading AI agents. Conceptually, the MCP is a wire connecting an agent to a tool (here, a proof assistant), which may need to be modified to accept the connection. Some proof assistants, like HOL Light, provide a simple command-line interface, sometimes called a REPL (for read-eval-print loop): the user types commands, and HOL Light replies. Connecting an agent to a REPL is easy. But most proof assistants provide sophisticated user interfaces, such as the Lean extension for Microsoft VS Code. That’s great for human users, but an AI agent needs something simple and direct. So we are proud to announce the following tools, which are publicly available in the AutoCorrode verification suite: I/Q: This enables an AI agent to communicate with a live Isabelle session running on your computers. It allows you to temporarily hand over control of the proof assistant to the AI to fill in some formal material or to assess the context and provide advice. I/R: This enables an agent to develop proofs or other formal material while the user keeps working with the proof assistant. The agent still “talks” directly to the proof assistant to know if its proofs work, but it does not take control the way I/Q does. Isabelle Assistant: Powered by I/Q, this provides an Isabelle user with a chat window to an AI agent, which can observe and modify the user’s session, developing or fixing proofs. It’s less powerful than the full I/Q and I/R package but runs in a convenient window, right out of the box. To get an idea of how effective AI is at solving mathematical problems, let’s look at some well-known examples, done automatically with the help of Isabelle Assistant. The square root of two is irrational The ancient Greeks were already aware that the square root of two could not be written as a fraction. Suppose that √2 = a/b is a fraction in lowest terms. Then 2b2 = a2, implying that a is even. But then a = 2k for some k. Then 2b2 = 4k2, so b2 = 2k2 and now b is even. But in that case, a/b is not a fraction in lowest terms. From this contradiction, we conclude that no such fraction exists. Here is the same proof, formalized for Isabelle by Claude Opus 4.6: As with all proof assistants, the language is designed to be checkable by computer. But it is also designed to be human-readable. Here is a little guide: assume introduces an assumption have and show claim some formula to be true obtain claims that certain values exist by gives the justification of a claim We use show when proving facts that we are committed to proving and have when proving facts that we need along the way. The justifications invoke proof methods, which typically refer to existing theorems, but we needn’t go into detail about those. Now we can read the code and see the mathematics. We start by assuming that √2 belongs to the set of rational numbers, ℚ. Then we obtain integers a and b, etc.; note that the coprime statement expresses that its two operands have no common factor. The proof continues to the ultimate contradiction as outlined above. This AI-generated proof is surprisingly idiomatic, though more detailed than strictly necessary. Finding N consecutive composite numbers The claim is that for every integer N > 0, there exists a block of N consecutive integers that are composite, i.e., that are not prime numbers. So although the primes go on forever, they are spaced further and further apart. This example is not so well known, so when proposing it to Claude, we also gave it the following proof: Take N! (N factorial, i.e., the product of the integers from 1 to N). N! + 2 must be even, N! + 3 must be divisible by 3, and so forth to N! + N. I hope you can spot what is wrong with this “proof”. When I supplied it to Claude, it came up with three facts. The first states that if k > 1 is a divisor of n > 0, then n + k is not prime. The second states that if 2 ≤ k ≤ N + 1, then (N + 1)! + k is not prime. And that is essentially our conclusion. But the third fact is the theorem presented in the correct form. Claude noticed that our proof gave us only N - 1 consecutive integers and made the necessary correction. Let’s skip the lemmas and just look at the main theorem: The theorem statement (after shows) is in symbolic form, but it expresses that there exists m such that m + i is composite for all i.Definite integral of the sine function Now for something a bit harder: calculus. Let’s look at the integral of the function sin x over the interval [0, π]. (For those of you who prefer degrees, π corresponds to 180°.) The integral is the shaded area below, and it equals two. In mathematical notation, the integral is written like this: But with an AI agent, you don’t have to know how to code such a thing in your favorite proof assistant. All we asked for was “a nice simple example involving calculus”, and a plain English description of the integral would have worked, too. Claude generated this (even the comments): As you may remember from calculus class — for most people the happiest time of their lives — evaluating this integral requires finding the antiderivative (say ƒ) of the sine function and evaluating ƒ(π) - ƒ(0). This fact is called the fundamental theorem of calculus. “Antiderivative” means a function whose derivative is sin x, which turns out to be -cos x. The Isabelle proof above includes a proof that the derivative of -cos x is sin x. The calculation is a bit longer than necessary, but at least it is error free, thanks to our approach of interleaving generation and checking. Harder projects These examples were easy. Much harder problems can still be formalized automatically by a good agent. To manage the toughest problems, we need I/Q and I/R. Through I/Q we can link an agent running in a terminal window to our Isabelle session, which it can edit directly. But through I/R, it can also create an Isabelle subprocess that works silently and invisibly to prove theorems and undertake other formalization tasks. Because it doesn’t touch the document, we can work at the same time. The AI agent becomes a partner who works for us and who can advise us but also accepts hints from us. It’s a new type of teamwork, and we still need to figure out how to make it work best. The hardest problems still require human thought, but thinking is hard work, and people get tired. Being able to direct an agent to carry out straightforward but lengthy and tiresome tasks — say, to refactor a working but messy proof development or study a trace to diagnose a problem — leaves us fresh enough to make key decisions when we must. I/R can be run standalone: we can set it up ourselves and direct it to run autonomously for a long time.

item.title: Using a "chaos loop" to harden the Claude Docs launch: 60 server errors across billions of requests
item.abstract: Three weeks before Claude Docs opened to the public, it was running as a proof of concept on a single node, used by a few thousand people inside Anthropic. We were racing toward an ambitious launch date, and our own estimate said we'd see millions of docs within the first few days. We launched on September 16. By September 22, people had created over 4.6 million docs. Across 2 billion requests we saw only 60 server errors, and we never had to roll back. The whole Docs service ran on about 50 memory-optimized pods. Two decisions got us there: A chaos loop at launch scale. We set up a test harness on our staging environment where Claude ran constantly for two weeks to try and break the service. It load tested every part of our infrastructure and fixed whatever fell over. Improving legibility to Claude. Claude could only close the loop effectively on fixes if our system produced accurate telemetry every iteration. We made a call early to avoid any runtime that uses memory or CPU in ways our code can't easily control (e.g. runtimes with garbage collection). When a telemetry signal looked concerning, Claude could easily trace it to a bug or a specific design decision. But honestly, this only worked because our frontier models have gotten much better recently (I used an internal research model roughly comparable to Claude Fable 5.2). In our experience, they can now stick with one goal through a run like this for weeks, which is what helped us hit launch scale in a tight timeline. THE CHAOS LOOP A few thousand internal users on one machine told us nothing about whether the service would survive launch, and we obviously didn't have launch traffic to test with. We wanted real evidence to decide how fast we could roll out. So on September 4, about two weeks before launch, I had Claude drive a staging cluster that mirrored production at over a million synthetic docs a day and break core components on purpose. And then... I just left it running (I've included the full cost at the end of this article). My setup was pretty simple. The loop was a session in Claude Code that I left running: pick a scenario, run the harness, read the telemetry, propose a fix, ship it to staging, repeat. That session acted as a coordinator and handed most of the work to sub-agents. In the busiest week, that usually meant about 11 sub-agents running at a time, and 30 at the peak. The coordinator also talked to our internal variant of Claude Tag (beta) via the Slack MCP to learn from other infrastructure teams at Anthropic who had scaled similar services. Their agents checked our scaling approach for pitfalls they’d already hit. The fun part was picking scenarios I thought were paranoid: 10M new docs created in a single day 22,000 live connections reconnecting at once One hot doc with hundreds of viewers, a server killed while it was still loading a doc, and the database stalling Each iteration looked the same. Our testing harness selected a feature like document creation and pushed creation to saturation. Claude then read telemetry using the Datadog MCP and came back with a short menu of options and a recommendation. If the recommendation was easy to undo, Claude wrote and deployed the change to staging and reran the test. We had telemetry on every operation the service ran. Every database query, for example, reported its name and how many rows it scanned versus how many it returned, so Claude could spot a bad query and rewrite it. FIG 1 One iteration of the loop, with two decisions made by a person Before the loop started, I told Claude which decisions needed my approval; basically anything hard to undo, like changing the database schema or key layout, or changing how a doc is stored and materialized. When Claude ran into one of those, it stopped and asked me, usually with a recommendation that I ended up approving. Schema changes were the classic case where I wanted to be consulted: there are usually a few reasonable answers, and changing directions is often painful. And during the whole testing process, Claude had to conform to two invariants: Docs had to open almost instantly (even ones with a long history) Once the server acknowledged an edit, tests had to show the edit was still there MAKING THE SERVICE LEGIBLE TO CLAUDE My colleague Felix Rieseberg recently wrote a tutorial on being more ambitious with models . His main idea is to raise the "altitude" you prompt Claude at: ask for the outcome you want, not the individual task. So instead of asking Claude to fix individual crashes, you ask it to make your app crash-free. (Our own apps aren't all the way there yet, but this is how we're making real progress.) To work at that altitude, though, you have to set up your code so Claude can pull crash reports on its own and run a harness that reproduces each crash and checks the fix. For us, the outcome was a service that could handle launch. To get there, we did two things to make the service as legible to Claude as we could: A diagnostic loop. Claude read the telemetry on every iteration and added whatever it thought was missing. Legible technology choices. We picked a runtime and dependencies so any number Claude measured traced back to code we wrote. A diagnostic loop Every iteration, Claude read the telemetry and added whatever it thought was missing. Writing telemetry by hand is tedious, so in practice most telemetry would go in after something broke. Now Claude just writes it as it goes. Memory is the best example. Early in the harness run, one large doc was using about 3 GB on its pod (not a fun number to see). Claude’s first stab at fixing it was to shrink one of our caches so our server would evict docs sooner. The next harness run showed the memory was actually in a separate cache inside one of our dependencies, so Claude dropped the change. From there Claude kept narrowing it down with finer-grained memory profiling. Eventually it found that every keystroke was copying the doc into several different data structures, adding a few MB each time. Claude switched those structures to copy-on-write, so they now share one reference instead of each holding its own copy. After about three days of iterating, that doc topped out around 180 MB, and our estimate of what we’d need for launch dropped from more than 500 memory-optimized pods to about 50. FIG 2 The diagnostic loop Legible technology choices We were picky about the service’s runtime and dependencies. We wanted any number Claude measured to trace back to code we wrote. This is because our models hill climb best with a clean signal. We expected a garbage collector to add noise, because memory and latency shift on the collector’s schedule. Two choices helped the most. We wrote the service in Rust . With no garbage collector, all of a doc’s memory sits in structures we defined, so when it grew, Claude could point to the one responsible, change it, and see whether memory came down on the next iteration. We have great Go tooling at Anthropic too, and we didn’t bake off the two languages, so this is our experience with Rust. What I did appreciate, coming from past work in Go, was how little I had to think about memory sticking around after my code was done with it. We also kept dependencies to a minimum . Every library brings data structures we didn’t write and can’t easily account for. For the few we really needed, we vendored the code so we could read and measure it ourselves. Rust is hard for people to write, and a few years ago that would have weighed heavily on the choice. Claude writes it and most other languages fine, so that matters a lot less now. FIG 3 Legible technology choices: memory our code can explain, and memory it can't LAUNCH WEEK The service held at launch scale. The first million docs showed up in about 30 hours, and we were past 4.6 million by September 22. We rolled prod 629 times in September and never once rolled back. Launch week felt weirdly familiar.

item.title: Introducing Gemini Decision 1: A Model That Picks Answers Instead of Writing Them
item.abstract: Introducing Gemini Decision 1: A Model That Picks Answers Instead of Writing Them Google's newest model has one job, and it never writes a word doing it. Decision 1 reads text, images, video, audio and PDFs in a single forward pass, up to 262,144 input tokens per request. By Shittu Olumide , Technical Content Specialist on November 18, 2026 in Artificial Intelligence Google's newest model has one job, and it never writes a word doing it. Gemini Decision 1 , launched last week with the new Gemini Decisions API , takes an input and a list of closed questions and returns probabilities instead of prose: yes or no, option A, B or C, a score on a rubric. That sounds small, but it isn't. Every agent stack runs on dozens of these quiet calls: which model gets this query, which tool fires, whether this message breaks a policy. Most teams handle them with a full generative model and a JSON parser, paying for output tokens they throw away. Google now sells that layer on its own, at \$0.10 per million input tokens and nothing for output. What Gemini Decision 1 Does Decision 1 reads text, images, video, audio and PDFs in a single forward pass, up to 262,144 input tokens per request. Against that one input, you can ask up to 1,000 independent questions of three kinds: Yes/no ( noul in the API) returns a probability between 0.01 and 0.99 Choice picks from 2 to 255 options and returns a probability for each Score grades against an ordered rubric and returns a weighted score plus a probability per level Every answer carries a confidence value, so your code can send uncertain cases to a fallback or a person. The pricing is the pitch. You pay \$0.10 per million input tokens , the shared input is billed once no matter how many questions you ask, and output costs nothing because there is none. A no-cost tier in Google AI Studio covers prototyping. The capability table shows what this model is not. Text generation, thinking, function calling, structured outputs, batch and caching are all listed as unsupported. It's a scoring engine, not a chatbot. What Happened When We Ran It? We installed Google's google-genai SDK, created a free API key in AI Studio and ran three tests: Google's quickstart, Google's image example from the launch post , and an ambiguous support message of our own. Latency was timed from our machine, so it includes the network round trip. The quickstart asks two questions about one customer message: from google import genai client = genai.Client(http_options={"api_version": "v1beta"}) result = client.decisions.create( model="gemini-decision-1", input="The blue mug I ordered on Monday arrived cracked on Wednesday.", questions={ "is_damaged": {"type": "noul", "instructions": "Did the item arrive damaged?"}, "queue": { "type": "choice", "instructions": "Which support queue should handle this message?", "criteria": { "billing": "Payment, invoice, or refund questions.", "replacements": "Damaged, missing, or wrong items.", "general": "Product questions and account updates.", }, }, }, ) print(result.answers["queue"].choice, result.answers["queue"].confidence) For the image test, input becomes a list holding an image URL and a text note. Here's what came back: Test Input Answer Median latency Input tokens Quickstart "Mug arrived cracked" Damaged: 0.99. Queue: replacements (0.98) 407 ms 173 Ambiguous "Charged twice, handle chipped" Damaged: 0.99. Queue: replacements 0.50, billing 0.48 574 ms 181 Image + text Breakroom counter photo Spill: 0.95. Action: wipe with cloth (0.98). Severity: 1.19 of 2 1,343 ms 1,326 Medians exclude each test's first call. Accuracy was clean: both of Google's examples came back right, and the image result matched Google's own screenshot . Every call billed zero output tokens. In dollars, the text query costs about \$0.000017 per call, roughly 58,000 calls for a dollar. The image query costs about \$0.00013 . Google Is Already Running on It Google says four of its own products use the Decisions API: Gemini Notebook routes each query to a model tier and thinking level, which Google says cuts latency on everyday queries by up to 40% Stitch uses it in its rapid canvas experiment to build playable wireframes and apply voice or tap edits CC from Google Labs picks an emoji reaction from more than 200 options without adding visible delay Google Search uses it as a safety layer that checks Model Context Protocol tools for adversarial behavior Our Take 1. The Confidence Score Is the Real Product Our ambiguous message is the test that matters. It fit two queues, and the model said so: 50.2% replacements, 48.4% billing, confidence 0.50. It didn't fake certainty on a coin flip, and in the same call it still rated the chipped handle as damage at 0.99. One example doesn't prove calibration, which is measured across thousands of cases. But it's the behavior Google is selling, and it showed up when we went looking for it. 2. Read Confidence, Not Just Choice Here's the trap. On that coin-flip message, the choice field still returned replacements , with no flag attached. Code that reads only the winner routes it as confidently as the clear case. The calibration is only worth something if you set a threshold on confidence and send everything below it elsewhere. Google's quickstart prints the winner. Your production code shouldn't stop there. 3. The Speed Claim Didn't Hold for Images Google quotes 150 to 250 ms end to end. After the first call, our text calls landed between 339 and 577 ms, a gap network distance can plausibly explain. Our image calls took 1.1 to 1.4 seconds, a median five to nine times the claim, though Google says its figures hold across multimodal inputs. Some of that may be Google fetching the image from a URL and processing 1,064 image tokens. We can't separate the causes from outside. Two more details: Google's latency figure covers contexts up to 16K tokens, not the full 256K, and identical calls in our runs varied by more than 300 ms. Benchmark it on your own media before it goes anywhere near a real-time path. 4. The Benchmarks Are Google's Own The "nearly 5x cheaper" figure compares Decision 1 with Google's own Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, on a benchmark suite Google chose . That's useful if you already run Gemini. It says nothing about how Decision 1 compares with a small fine-tuned classifier you already have. 5. Check the Small Print The model page pitches classification over live media streams, while the same page lists the Live API as unsupported. And the model is Gemini-only for now. It's on OpenRouter , LangChain , Vercel's AI SDK , LiteLLM and others, but Google Cloud support is still marked as coming soon . Wrapping Up Decision 1 does one narrow job well. It's cheap, it was accurate on everything we gave it, and it admitted doubt when we pushed it. Use it for routing and policy checks now. Wire your code to confidence from the first day, and time it on your own images before you promise anyone 200 ms. item.title: Energy-Based Reasoners: 385x more efficient inference
item.abstract:
Looping is a powerful inductive bias for reasoning. By repeatedly iterating a recurrent block, looped models can scale their effective depth and enable multi-step reasoning in latent space. However, existing looped models are not inherently guided by an explicit measure of progress, making it difficult to determine when to stop looping and how to improve upon the current state. To enable this, we introduce Energy-Based Reasoners ( EBRs ), which learn an energy function over latent reasoning states and formulate looped updates as gradient descent on this energy. The energy scores latent states, while its gradient guides refinement and provides a signal for stopping. To train EBRs effectively, we further introduce exploration-based training to discover additional modes and to better shape the energy landscape over a broader set of states. Across four algorithmic reasoning benchmarks, EBRs match or outperform prior recurrent reasoning models, achieving 99.9% accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme while using 345× less inference compute than the next-best model and maintaining comparable training compute. On all multi-solution benchmarks, EBRs achieve state-of-the-art coverage of distinct valid solutions while maintaining near-100% single-sample accuracy. These results suggest that energy-based models are a promising approach for strong reasoning performance.

item.title: SID AI Releases SID-2 Agentic Search Model With 0.720 NDCG Swarm Mode
item.abstract: SID AI has released SID-2 , its second-generation agentic search model, alongside SID-2 Swarm. SID-2 is an agentic search model from SID AI that searches your data, reads results and returns ranked document IDs. It replaces fixed RAG pipelines with a model that decides what to search next. SID-2 is a small search specialist, not a general chat model. A static pipeline runs rewrite, embed, search and rerank in a fixed order. SID-2 instead searches, reads results, adapts and searches again . Developers implement the search tools against their own backend. A text_search tool covers keyword search and a search tool covers vector search. The model ends each episode by calling report_helpful_ids with a ranked list. No reindexing or data movement is required , since SID-2 only sees what your tools return. SID-2 Swarm runs several agents that message each other and fork their context into new agents. Each agent explores a separate slice of the corpus. SID argues search gains more from reading more documents than from reasoning harder about each one. SID-2 offers low, medium and high reasoning effort. Each level was trained as a separate expert, then merged with multi-teacher on-policy distillation. Metric Steering lets users target NDCG, F1 or Recall@k, with k from 1 to 50. On SID’s 506-question validation set, SID-2 at high effort scores 0.14 to 0.22 higher per metric than the base model. Training used 2-stage reinforcement learning. Stage 1 optimizes retrieval quality only. Stage 2 adds a multiplicative latency penalty that applies only to positive rewards. A proposer-solver self-play loop generated hard queries against a frozen SID-1 solver. SID reports a 6x training-throughput gain over SLIME’s default setup. SID built a 506-question benchmark across 19 corpora. These include HotpotQA, Enron emails, SEC filings, PubMed and BrowseComp-Plus. All numbers below are self-reported from Tables 2 to 4 of the report . Swarm leads on 11 of 19 corpora. On WixQA, a single high-effort agent matches Astra at about 232x lower cost. At its lowest effort, SID-2 beats 4 parallel SID-1 runs with 13x fewer FLOPs. NDCG, time and cost rows are measured by SID on its own benchmark. Retrieval backend time is excluded. SID-2 is available through SID’s API and on Baseten . SDKs exist for Python ( sid-sdk ), TypeScript ( @sid-ai/sid-sdk ) and Go ( github.com/sidhq/sid-go ). A SageMaker helper covers AWS deployments. The reference implementation uses the OpenAI client format. SID-2 costs $0.25 per million input tokens and $1.00 per million output tokens . Swarm costs $0.50 and $2.00. Cached input is 10% of the input price. Check out the SID-2 technical report , the docs and the model page . item.title: 180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers
item.abstract:
Back to Articles 180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers Published November 18, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 5 Tarek Ziadé tarekziade Follow Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation. I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally.
At home I have a PC with two RTX 4090s (let's call it Orthrus - the two-headed hound
of Greek mythology), and for work I have a MacBook M5 with 32G of unified memory. Orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time. I had a
dual boot with Ubuntu, but their games ended up taking most of the two
terabytes of disk. I am also a huge fan of RMD (rooms moving development): one hour in the kitchen
sipping my coffee, two hours at my office desk, then the sofa. A fixed desktop
tower is not for me. My first experiment was to run Qwen 3.8 27B with llama.app on Orthrus and use
it from my laptop through pi . That model does the coding tasks, an online
model like Opus does the orchestration, and the second RTX runs a FIM model for
auto-completion in Neovim. When I talked about this on social networks, I got very strong feedback: use Strata with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next . What is Strata? Strata is an inference engine for MoE models like Qwen. Only the hot experts
stay in VRAM, the rest goes to RAM, or even to disk. Experts are 90%+ of a MoE
model's weights, so a 180B model like this one can run on a GPU with much less
memory. Like my RTX 4090! It works on a laptop too, and I stumbled on this blog post doing
exactly that: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac M4, faster than llama.cpp , at
13.5 tok/s. That's too slow for how I use coding agents, but it's an interesting itch to
scratch. A whole range of MoE models don't fit in a MacBook's unified memory and
could run at a decent speed. How do other engines offload? Before committing to Strata, I looked at what llama.cpp, vLLM and Transformers do when a MoE model doesn't fit. Three questions matter: where do the experts
live, where does the expert matmul run, and what moves on each token? llama.cpp maps the GGUF file with mmap and can keep the experts on the
CPU ( --cpu-moe , --n-cpu-moe N , -ot "exps=CPU" , or --fit on to pick for
you). Those experts are also computed on the CPU, so only the activations
cross PCIe, never the weights. Great when the experts fit in RAM. When they
don't, the page cache thrashes. A GPU expert cache ( --moe-cache-mib ) just
landed, but it fragments the graph (2 splits per token become 50) and loses
~10% even when everything fits. vLLM 's --cpu-offload-gb N puts N GB of weights in pinned RAM, and kernels
read them in place over PCIe. For a MoE layer, that's only the routed experts,
but nothing is cached: a hot expert crosses PCIe again on every token, and
there's no disk tier. By default the offloaded weights include dense layers,
read on every token; --cpu-offload-params experts keeps it to the experts. That fits vLLM's big
batches, which touch almost every expert anyway, less so one user on one GPU. Transformers offloads through Accelerate ( device_map="auto" , offload_folder ), one module at a time: hooks copy its weights to the GPU
before forward . For a MoE, that module is a layer's whole expert bank, so
every token copies every expert of every offloaded layer to use 8 or 10 of them.
No cache, no notion of routing. And on a Mac, CPU and GPU share the same memory,
so "offload to CPU" frees nothing. I ran all of them on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on one A10G (24 GB), with plenty of RAM,
and Harry Mellor reran vLLM with better flags: Engine Decode (tok/s) Strata, Q8_0 82 - 88 llama.cpp, Q8_0, --fit on 63 - 64 llama.cpp, BF16, --fit on 35 - 36 vLLM, FP8, --cpu-offload-gb 16 --cpu-offload-params experts 20.1 vLLM, FP8, same flags, --enforce-eager 14.7 vLLM, FP8, --cpu-offload-gb 16 9.7 vLLM, BF16, --cpu-offload-gb 50 --cpu-offload-params experts 7.3 vLLM, BF16, --cpu-offload-gb 50 3.3 Transformers + Accelerate 0.16 Offloading only the experts doubles vLLM's speed, and FP8 helps on top (half
the bytes per expert, more of the model on the GPU). vLLM's other offload
backend, which copies groups of layers ahead of time, ran under 1 tok/s. If the experts fit in RAM, llama.cpp is hard to beat. If they don't, you have to
stream only what the router picks, through a bounded cache, fast enough that the
SSD is the bottleneck and not Python, ideally reusing the model's fast expert
kernels. That's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac, and Transformers couldn't do
it out of the box. Making Qwen3.8-Flash-Next work on my 32 GB Mac with Transformers Strata was already too slow for me on the laptop, and Transformers was not going
to beat it anytime soon. But the Accelerate path was so far off that I wanted to
try fixing offloading in Transformers itself, with the big model on my laptop as
the target, knowing it would probably stay too slow for how I work. All of the code was built with AI: the Transformers PR, the model-specific
package and the Metal kernels. My part was choosing what to try, reading the
profiles, and deciding what to keep. Everything is in a Space: tarekziade/moe-expert-streaming . Start small I started with OLMoE-1B-7B , which fits in memory, so I could compare every token
with vanilla Transformers. First version: experts on disk, an LRU cache on the device, and a Python loop
running one expert at a time. With every expert already cached, it did 10.1
tok/s. Vanilla did ~32. The I/O was fine, my loop was not: vanilla uses grouped_mm , which runs all the experts of a layer in one kernel. The fix, and the key idea of this project, was to turn the cache into a slot
pool : one preallocated device tensor shared by all layers, plus a per-layer
table from expert id to slot. Remap the router's expert ids to slots and the
pool looks like a regular expert bank, so grouped_mm runs on it as is. No
custom expert matmul needed. That got it to 34.6 tok/s, against 38.1 for
vanilla. experts_offload I then turned the standalone loader into an option of from_pretrained , in huggingface/transformers#50717 .
To try it, install Transformers from that PR: pip install "git+https://github.com/huggingface/transformers.git@refs/pull/50717/head" Then, moving from OLMoE to the real target, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next: path = snapshot_download( "tarekziade/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-expert-streaming" ) model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( f" {path} /dense" , dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map={ "" : "mps" , "experts.*" : "disk" }, quantization_config=MetalConfig(bits= 8 ), experts_offload={ "cache_bytes" : 12 << 30 , "quantized_experts" : f" {path} /experts-q3" , },
) That repo holds the output of the project's conversion script :
the dense weights, the experts quantized to 3 bits, and the n-gram table. Experts mapped to "disk" go through the streaming path instead of Accelerate's
offload: the loader skips their tensors and MoE layers switch to an offloaded
implementation. Misses are read by 8 I/O threads, one contiguous read per
expert. The next two layers' routers run early on the current hidden states to
guess which experts to prefetch. Experts can be quantized offline so reads are
smaller. It works for MoE models with the standard experts layout. The API is still being discussed with the Transformers maintainers. The device_map form came out of that, and quantized experts will probably go
through the per-layer quantization plan of #50245 rather than
their own option. Running 121 GB of experts on a 32 GB Mac Qwen3.8-Flash-Next has 48 layers of 512 experts (10 active), 121 GB in FP8.
Streaming them isn't enough: there's also a 51 GB n-gram embedding
table that needs its own disk path. So: experts quantized to 3 bits: 49 GB on disk, 12 GiB cached on the device dense layers in 8 bits (~5.4 GB, +0.2% perplexity vs BF16) the n-gram table stays on disk, rows read when needed The conversion takes ~5 hours. After loading, it uses ~18 GiB, and a 6K prompt
peaks at 25.4 GiB.

item.title: New LoRA Adapter Lifts Qwen3.8 Coding Success From 39% to 65%
item.abstract: Hugging Face’s harness-hub team has released Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted , a LoRA adapter for Qwen3.8-27B . It was trained with reinforcement learning to work inside the pi coding agent . The Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted LoRA adapter targets one harness instead of general chat. For developers running local coding agents, that is the point. You keep the open base model and swap in a small, harness-specific adapter. Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted is a PEFT LoRA adapter that turns Qwen3.8-27B into a model tuned for pi. pi is an MIT-licensed agent toolkit with a coding agent CLI. The adapter is released under Apache-2.0 . It applies to the q, k, v, o, gate, up and down projections. It only works on Qwen3.8-27B. The base model is a dense hybrid . It alternates Gated DeltaNet linear-attention blocks with Gated Attention blocks across 64 layers. The method comes from Hugging Face’s harness adapters post from November 6. The idea is 1 LoRA adapter per model and harness. Training runs inside the unmodified harness on verifiable tasks. For this checkpoint, the model card lists these details: Every tool call passes through safeagents , a rule-based proxy. It blocks calls such as fetching benchmark answers from the Hub. Blocked rollouts score 0, so RL pushes the model away from reward hacking. All numbers below are self-reported. They use the pi harness, 1 attempt per task. The adapter solved 15 new SWE-bench Pro tasks and lost 2. On Terminal-Bench 2.1, it gained 16 and lost 2. Efficiency is the larger story. On tasks both models solved, median turns fell from 59 to 23 on SWE-bench Pro. On Terminal-Bench 2.1, they fell from 18 to 8. The adapter also generates about 4.5x fewer tokens than the base model with thinking. With thinking on, the base model already scores 64.7% on SWE-bench Pro and 54.2% on Terminal-Bench 2.1. So the adapter matches thinking-level accuracy without paying for long reasoning traces. With thinking on, the adapter reaches 66.7% and 56.6%. OpenCode adapter numbers use a different harness and are not directly comparable. item.title: Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review
item.abstract:
Editor’s Note: Engineers at firms that adopted AI coding agents added about 30 percent more code, yet finished work did not measurably rise and getting code through review took 49 percent longer, according to a working paper by Harvard Ph.D. candidates Fiona Chen and James Stratton covering 718 firms. The paper, a job-market paper with no indication of completed peer review, measures what happens at the human checkpoint once drafting speeds up. Harvey’s motion-to-dismiss workflow and Cooley’s redaction agent, still in development with Google Cloud, both keep a lawyer at a comparable checkpoint, and neither announcement reports a measure of that review stage. For eDiscovery, privacy and compliance professionals, the study suggests a measurement approach for legal AI buyers: consider approved work product, revision rates and reviewer time alongside drafting output. It also shows that AI authorship can leave metadata in collaboration systems that records and legal hold programs may need to reach. Watch for a revised version of the paper and for any legal vendor that publishes review-stage figures, keeping in mind that the study examined software, not legal work. Content Assessment: Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review Information - 92% Insight - 90% Relevance - 88% Objectivity - 90% Authority - 92% 90 % Excellent A short percentage-based assessment of the qualitative benefit expressed as a percentage of positive reception of the recent article from ComplexDiscovery OÜ titled, "Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review." News Analysis – Artificial Intelligence Beat Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review ComplexDiscovery OÜ Staff Engineers at firms that adopted AI coding agents added about 30 percent more code, but finished work did not measurably rise and getting code through review took 49 percent longer, a Harvard working paper found. In the study’s data, the extra coding produced no detectable rise in finished work, and code review became the bottleneck. Fiona Chen and James Stratton, both Ph.D. candidates at Harvard University, measured that pattern across 725,938 workers at 718 companies. Two legal AI announcements this month, Harvey’s motion-to-dismiss workflow and a court-filing redaction agent Cooley is developing with Google Cloud, place a lawyer at a comparable review step, and neither reports a measure of it. What the Harvard data measured How much weight that pattern can bear depends on where the numbers came from. Chen and Stratton built the study on data from Jellyfish, a company that sells an analytics platform tracking engineering activity, and joined it to LinkedIn employment records collected by Revelio Labs. The sample runs from January 2021 to March 2026 and covers Jellyfish client firms that consented to research use of their data. The paper’s tables list 68.3 million Jira issues, 200.9 million commits, 49.1 million pull requests and 21.3 million calendar events, though only 213 of the 718 firms supplied calendar data. The design is a staggered difference-in-differences comparison, which tracks month by month how outcomes changed at adopting firms against firms that had not yet adopted. A comparison like that is only as good as the reasons adoption dates differed, and here the authors point to a process legal and security teams will recognize, because they sit inside it. The paper says timing was shaped mainly by when firms learned about the tools and by how long procurement took, meaning sourcing, legal and security approvals and pilot programs. One interviewee’s firm approved a tool in about a day; another interviewee put the average approval time at six to 12 months. The authors call those procurement delays plausibly unrelated to how fast a firm was growing, which they argue supports comparing early and late adopters. They acknowledge one known imbalance, that larger firms adopted earlier, and they control for firm size. If some hidden difference remains, the authors say, it would more likely make AI look more productive than it is, not less. A bias in that direction would make the flat output result, if anything, generous to AI. The current version of the paper is dated Aug. 4, 2026, and the first was dated Jan. 7. Chen circulated it as her job-market paper, and nothing in the version reviewed for this article indicates journal acceptance or completed peer review. Her website lists coverage links to The Wall Street Journal and The Economist, and legal trade press picked it up this month, including an Oct. 12 eDiscovery Today post by Doug Austin that relayed an Ars Technica report. Drafts went up and finished issues did not With that provenance in view, the coding results are large. Lines of code added rose by 1,494 per worker-month against a baseline of 5,017, about 30 percent. Commits rose 20 percent, and pull requests, the bundles of code submitted for review, rose 23 percent. The authors note that these estimates capture the added effect of agents at firms that already had AI coding assistants, not the effect of AI from a standing start. Output is where the gain stops. The paper counts finished work as Jira issues resolved, and an issue counts as complete when its code is deployed to production. Agents moved that measure by 0.12 issues per worker-month on a 3.67 baseline, with a standard error of 0.17. That result is statistically indistinguishable from zero, and the 95 percent confidence interval rules out an increase above about 12 percent of the baseline, well short of the 30 percent rise in code written. The authors tested the obvious escape route. If engineers had shifted to larger tasks, a flat issue count would understate real output. So the researchers labeled a 0.5 percent sample of issues by size with GPT-4o and extended those labels to every issue with a text-embedding model. They found no shift in average issue size, and pull requests did not grow larger either, which the authors use to set aside the simplest explanation for what happened in review. Where the shortfall shows up: the review queue The paper locates the shortfall in code review. The time from pull request submission to merge rose 3.45 days on a 7.03-day baseline, a 49 percent increase. The share of pull requests receiving a formal change request increased by about 12 percentage points from a baseline of 13 percent, nearly doubling, and review comments per pull request rose 35 percent. The share of workers doing any code review rose 14 percent from a base of about 29 percent, while the share writing code showed no measurable change. AI review tools did not remove the bottleneck. By March 2026, nearly 80 percent of the firms had used one, yet AI generated only 23.3 percent of review comments, and only 10.8 percent of pull requests received even one AI comment. The authors write that the bottleneck persists after firms adopt such tools. The paper’s interviews show what that looks like on a team: a junior software engineer described a project where only one senior engineer could approve changes and could review the interviewee’s code only once a week. “After some outages that were caused by AI-generated commits, there were also new rules requiring senior engineer approval for AI-generated code, which created even more review bottlenecks,” the engineer said, in a quote the authors say they lightly edited for clarity. That account fits the model the authors use to explain their numbers, which has two channels. In the first, faster drafting sends more code to a fixed pool of reviewers, a problem that moving labor into review can largely relieve. In the second, the rise in change requests and comments, which faster drafting alone does not explain, reads through the model as a sign of lower-quality drafts. That problem, the authors say, would require better technology.

item.title: Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoints now support KV cache aware routing
item.abstract: Today, Amazon SageMaker AI introduces KV cache-aware routing (KV-aware routing), a new routing strategy for real-time endpoints. It uses the cache state that the model container reports. It sends each request to an instance that already holds a long cached match for its prompt and isn’t too busy. It’s for teams that serve large language models (LLMs) with multi-turn conversations, long shared prompts, or heavy load. You turn it on in two places: add one environment variable to your model so the container reports its cache contents, and set RoutingStrategy to KV_AWARE in the endpoint configuration. Your clients call the endpoint with the same APIs as before. Here’s the problem it solves: LLM applications such as chat assistants, Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), and agents with long system prompts send many requests that start with the same text. A model keeps the work it did on a prompt in GPU memory, the KV cache, and skips that work when the same start reaches the same instance again. In part 1 of this series , we introduced prefix-aware routing for Amazon SageMaker AI, which sends requests that start the same way to the same instance. Prefix-aware routing infers where a prefix is cached from the request alone, so it can’t tell when an instance has evicted that cache. Prefix-aware routing picks an instance from the request alone. It hashes the start of the request, up to the PrefixLength you configure (bytes of the InvokeEndpoint payload, or characters of the message text for the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API), and sends requests that start the same way to the same instance. It never sees what an instance actually has cached. This works well when every request starts with the same shared text, and less well in two cases: The cache on an instance changes over time. An instance evicts older KV cache entries when its GPU memory fills up, but the router keeps sending matching requests there as if the cache were still warm. A conversation starts out short. In a multi-turn chat, each turn adds to the history. While the request is still shorter than PrefixLength , every new turn changes the text the router hashes, so the next turn can land on a different instance than the one that cached the earlier turns. The turns of a conversation stay on one instance only after the request grows past PrefixLength . In this post, we explain how KV-aware routing works, when to use it, and how to enable, invoke, and verify it on single model endpoints and inference component endpoints. KV-aware routing has three parts: the model container reports what it has cached, SageMaker AI keeps a managed cache index of that state for the endpoint, and the endpoint uses the index to choose an instance for each request. When you turn events on with SM_VLLM_KV_EVENTS_CONFIG , the container publishes a KV cache event each time it stores or evicts cache entries, and SageMaker AI uses these events to keep the index current. The index holds only pointers: one-way, truncated hashes of cached content, each mapped to the instance or inference component copy that holds it. It never stores prompts, token IDs, request payloads, or KV tensors. When a request arrives, the endpoint tokenizes the prompt and looks up the tokens in the index. The index returns the instances or inference component copies that hold part of the prompt in their cache, and how much of it each one holds. For example, if instance A holds the cached start of a conversation, the next turn of that conversation goes to A. Because the index matches on tokens rather than a fixed number of bytes, a multi-turn history can match in full as it grows. A request that shares only part of its prompt still goes to the instance with the longest match. The endpoint then picks among these candidates by weighing how much of the prompt each one has cached against how busy it is. A candidate that is too busy is skipped, so if the instance with the longest match is busy, the request goes to the next-best one that is available. If no candidate has a useful match or all of them are busy, the request falls back to load-aware routing, as described in Routing overhead and fallbacks. You don’t configure a concurrency threshold for this, as you do with prefix-aware routing. The index also follows the fleet. When you scale in, entries for removed instances are dropped. When you scale out or an update replaces instances, the new instances start with empty caches, so latency can be higher for a short time. Figure 1: KV-aware routing on a SageMaker AI endpoint. The router looks up the managed cache index and forwards the request to the instance that holds the longest cached match. Each instance reports KV cache events back to the index In Figure 1, the endpoint has three instances, A, B, and C. Each instance runs the same model in its own model container (the AWS vLLM Deep Learning Container listed in Requirements and limits) and has its own KV cache in GPU memory, so each instance holds different cached content: A holds turns 1 to 3 of conversation 1, B holds conversations 2 and 3, and C holds document 7. When turn 4 of conversation 1 arrives (step 1), the router tokenizes it and looks it up in the managed cache index (step 2). The index shows that A holds the first 6,000 of the request’s 6,200 tokens, so the router sends the request to A (step 3), and A only has to compute the remaining tokens. If A is busy, the router sends the request to the least busy instance instead (step 4). KV-aware routing needs a choice of destinations, so it is active only with at least two instances, or at least two copies of an inference component. With a single instance, every request goes to that instance and the setting has no effect. With this launch, SageMaker AI offers four routing strategies for real-time endpoints. You set the strategy per production variant in the RoutingConfig of your endpoint configuration. Both strategies send requests to where their prefix is likely to be cached. They differ in how they know where that is, and in what they need from your container. We measured KV-aware routing against random routing in two ways: a large-scale benchmark on production-sized instances, and a smaller, reproducible comparison you can follow in Verify that KV-aware routing is working. In our benchmarks with Llama 3.1 70B Instruct on seven ml.p5.48xlarge instances, we ran 30-minute tests with 20 or 100 simulated users holding multi-turn chats and document Q&A sessions, with prompts of up to about 64,000 tokens. Compared with random routing, and with long prompts under load, KV-aware routing reduced p50 time to first token (TTFT) by up to 97 percent and increased throughput by up to 234 percent. It raised the KV cache hit rate from 3–48 percent to 80–93 percent. Long prompts gained even at lower load. The gain was smallest with short prompts, where there is less prefill to save. Results depend on your workload. To measure them for your own traffic, use the checks in Verify that KV-aware routing is working. Before it routes a request, the endpoint tokenizes the prompt and looks it up in the managed cache index. The lookup takes a few milliseconds for short prompts and longer for long ones, mostly for tokenization, but it stays small next to the time a cache hit saves. For text-only requests that use standard options, the tokens it computes are passed to the model, so the prompt isn’t tokenized twice. If the lookup is slow, finds no useful match, or all matching instances are busy, the endpoint routes the request with load-aware routing, the same behavior as the LEAST_OUTSTANDING_REQUESTS strategy. The request is still served, without the cache benefit. The same happens when the endpoint can’t tokenize a request, except in the two error cases described in Invoking the endpoint.

item.title: Reducing token costs and latency in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore JSON workloads
item.abstract: As enterprises build production agents with dozens of tools and large structured inputs, token consumption and latency become the primary blockers to a good user experience. When these agents process large JSON data, every additional tool invocation injects the full payload into the large language model (LLM) context window, causing token usage and response latency to spike. Over multi-turn conversations, this pressure compounds, driving up costs and degrading response quality. Effectively managing context-window pressure in agentic systems is key to reliability and responsiveness at scale. In this post, we share three composable strategies we used to build a production agent for Flightscape that handles 20 MB+ JSON payloads. You can apply them to reduce token costs, lower latency, and maintain full reasoning capability across extended sessions. Together, these optimizations reduced token consumption by up to 71% and cut average latency by up to 80% across our benchmark runs on a representative 23 MB payload. Flightscape is an airline operations platform that helps airlines plan and manage their crews, flights, and operations. As part of Flightscape’s crew management capabilities, we built a Training Schedule Optimization agent that verifies crew training schedule assignments against business rules. With 40+ tools and JSON inputs in megabytes, this agent could answer complex queries across crew assignments, scheduling, and resource allocation. Although the agent delivered the required functionality, average request latencies exceeded 15 seconds across most calls. Every tool call injected its full payload into the model context, inflating token counts and costs. On larger datasets, the context window filled up before the agent could finish reasoning. The following diagram (Figure 1) details the agentic architecture and data flow: Figure 1: Agent architecture and data flow In Figure 1, the Optimizer receives a Request JSON and produces a Response JSON, which is then validated by a Business Rules Validator to generate a Validation Report JSON. All three JSON documents are ingested by an AI Agent that provides a conversational interface for users to query optimization results, understand validation errors, and explore scheduling assignments. The agent is built with LangGraph , an open source framework by LangChain, and runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails can be applied to validate and filter the agent’s conversational responses, helping facilitate responsible AI practices in production deployments. We defined a custom agent state that holds the data needed by our tools: optimization request JSON, optimization response JSON, and validation report JSON. We also added basic statistics and cache data to state for rich queries. The agent uses an Amazon Bedrock model for reasoning and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to persist chat interactions across turns, and each turn follows this flow (Figure 2): This is what the state structure looks like. The state references TOPT (Training Optimizer) request and response objects, which represent the crew scheduling inputs and optimization results: Note: This state originally held heavy payloads inline. Later sections explain how we moved large artifacts out of conversational context to reduce token usage. We implemented three strategies to reduce the token costs, latency, and memory overhead caused by passing large JSON payloads through the model context. The following diagram (Figure 3) shows how the three strategies fit into a single agent turn. Strategy 1 runs at the start and end of each turn, and Strategies 2 and 3 run each time a tool returns a result. Figure 3: Overview of the three optimization strategies in one agent turn At the start of a turn, the hydrate_state() function restores lightweight session state from AgentCore memory. When a tool returns an oversized list or dictionary, the agent stores the full result in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and passes the model a compact summary with a handle. The model can then retrieve more detail with get_result_page_tool() . At the end of the turn, the dehydrate_state() function writes heavy payloads to the S3ArtifactStore and saves only references to AgentCore memory. The following sections describe each strategy in detail. To implement these strategies, make sure the following are in place: The companion code is available in this GitHub repository . Our first optimization was to change how we persist session state. Initially, large payloads were being stored too close to the conversational state. We therefore moved heavy artifacts (request JSON, response JSON, validation data, and other large derived payloads) to Amazon S3. AgentCore memory then persists only stable references to these objects, keeping the session state lightweight. To support this, we introduced a dedicated persisted-state schema that keeps only lightweight fields and artifact references. The live graph state still includes parsed domain objects for tool execution, but persistence now writes a dehydrated form. At runtime, tools hydrate heavy payloads on demand using those references, instead of loading everything on every turn. This PersistedState schema is what gets written to AgentCore Memory: The updated GraphState mirrors these references alongside the live domain objects: The dehydrate_state function strips heavy payloads from the live state and returns the lightweight persisted form along with the artifacts to upload: Rehydration reverses this process. When a session resumes, we rebuild the live graph state: deserialize LangChain messages, re-parse raw payloads into domain objects, and restore every reference key so later turns can locate their artifacts: Both dehydration and rehydration rely on the artifact store returning a consistent reference for each payload. Instead of minting a random key, we derive the reference from the payload itself. This approach, known as content addressing, serializes the JSON with sorted keys and compact separators, and uses the SHA-256 digest of those bytes as the reference. The _content_hash helper produces a deterministic SHA-256 reference from a JSON-serializable payload: Content addressing makes writes idempotent. Identical payloads map to the same key, so a turn that re-serializes an unchanged request JSON reuses the object already in the bucket instead of uploading it again. The S3-backed store exposes a put_json and get_json interface. It also keeps a small in-process cache, so payloads already read or written during the current invocation do not require a second S3 round trip. The S3ArtifactStore class wraps the put_json / get_json interface with an in-process cache and content-addressed keys: Offloading heavy artifacts to S3 and persisting only lightweight references reduced per-turn latency and the volume of data stored in AgentCore memory. With heavy payloads no longer persisted inline, tool-call responses became the dominant consumer of context tokens, prompting us to introduce result paging. Even after moving heavy payload persistence to Amazon S3, we still had a major token bottleneck at tool-response time. Many tool results were too large, which created two problems. First, we were sending full lists to the model even when it only needed a small subset, making each turn slower and more expensive. Second, those full list payloads were injected into context, which quickly consumed the context window over multi-turn conversations. In some cases, a single tool response exceeded 80,000 tokens, and the cost compounded as users continued interacting with the agent. We wanted to preserve full data access without sending everything by default. To solve this, we introduced on-demand result paging for large tool outputs.

item.title: How Airbnb uses cost per task to operate coding agents on Amazon Bedrock
item.abstract: Amazon Bedrock provides access to foundation models from multiple providers through a common API, with AWS managing the model infrastructure. It integrates with AWS access controls and monitoring, and processes prompts, code, and model responses within AWS. As coding agents move into production, changes in models and usage can affect latency, capacity, and cost. Amazon Bedrock runtime metrics in Amazon CloudWatch help teams investigate latency increases, throttling, and changes in token consumption. Evaluations, or evals, complement these operational metrics by assessing the quality of an agent’s work on a fixed set of representative tasks. In this post, we show how Airbnb evaluates models for coding agents and monitors their use on Amazon Bedrock. We explain how cost per task guides model selection and how production data helps us revisit those choices as usage changes.
