item.title: Cloudflare Joins the Jevolution and Labels Itself a Neolab
item.abstract: Cloudflare has been one of the essential infrastructure companies of the web for the past decade and a half. But now, it’s turning into a neolab — at least according to a presentation at AI Engineer Code Summit by Michelle Chen , who runs Cloudflare’s AI Platform on the product side. We’ll get into what exactly a neolab is in a minute (the short version: they build models and they’re not called OpenAI or Anthropic). Cloudflare is claiming to be one because it too has begun to launch models. Two System One models , to be precise: Clef and Clairic. As Chen explained in her talk, Clef is a decision model directly inspired by TypeSafe AI’s revolutionary Jev model , while Clairic is a new type of system one model that Cloudflare calls an “extract” model . In an interview with Latent Space after her presentation, Chen hinted that Cloudflare won’t just be producing system one models. There will be large language models, too. “We're not being a neolab [to] only launch system one models, even though it makes sense for our infrastructure. We've kind of entered this Pandora's box now, right? We opened it, now the possibilities are endless.” Chen said it’s “not just system one models, but potentially reasoning models that we've been experimenting with, and other LLMs and whatnot.” However, she added that these probably won’t be pre-trained models built from scratch, like the frontier labs produce. “I don't think that's our focus, but I think we can take existing resources out there and make [them] a lot more efficient and effective.” She noted that “most of our team really just does post-training,” so that will be the focus in model development. The term neolab literally means a ‘new lab’ and it was coined last November by Stephanie Palazzolo from The Information, who defined it as “a new generation of research-focused AI startups.” Deedy Das , a partner at Menlo Ventures and an AI influencer, runs a big list of neolabs . It includes companies like Thinking Machines Lab, Poolside, and TypeSafe AI itself. According to Das, neolabs employ elite researchers, spend a lot of compute (“usually to train its own AI model”), don't have significant revenue traction, and they’re typically startups that have raised a lot of money. Deedy Das’ list of neolabs — note that TypeSafe is among the top 20. Cloudflare doesn’t tick at least half of those boxes, since it’s a public company with significant revenue traction . In fact, earlier this month Cloudflare announced record earnings . “The third quarter was Cloudflare's best quarter ever,” said CEO Matthew Prince . “We crossed $3 billion in annualized revenue with revenue of $782 million, up 39% year over year.” So Cloudflare as a “neolab” is pushing the accepted definition. However, as Chen argued in her presentation, building models is part of a natural progression for the company : from infrastructure, to compute (e.g. the Workers platform, including now for agents), to storage, to serving open weight models like Kimi, GLM and DeepSeek (on Workers AI), to now building its own models. Chen readily admits that Jev inspired Cloudflare’s pivot to building models. Referencing a Chinese proverb, she framed Jev’s arrival in September as “the east wind” that unexpectedly changed how Cloudflare viewed AI models. “And so when the system one and Jev paradigm started coming on board,” Chen said in her presentation, “we were like, this makes so much sense for us to adopt, right? We don't have to send every request to an LLM. We can send some of it to a System One model.” In our conversation, Chen commented on how it took only two weeks for them to build Clef — which is a copy of Jev — whereas it took TypeSafe AI two years to build Jev. She meant that as a compliment for how hard TypeSafe AI worked to create this new type of model. “All credit to TypeSafe, really, for actually attacking this space and inventing something new here , that people could relate to so strongly and be able to use it. And, yeah, we came up with a model super quickly, but they put in a lot of legwork and we knew exactly what the API schema should look like and whatnot.” Cloudflare is, at its core, still an infrastructure company — speed and low latency is its meat and potatoes. The main benefit of System One models, Chen remarked, is that they allow more work to be done by smaller, faster models , where output is measured in milliseconds rather than seconds. While Clef was a clone of Jev, Cloudflare soon came up with an original twist on System One with Clairic , launched last month as “the first model in a new class: System One extraction models.” “What Clairic does is it can take unstructured input, and it can extract, compute, estimate and forecast values from those inputs,” Chen explained in her presentation. In our interview, Chen said that her team wanted to use System One principles to find other areas where LLMs were “overkill” and didn’t always return the right answer. One of the problems they settled on was that LLMs don’t always deal well with unstructured input. Because LLMs are autoregressive, Chen explained, they are prone to hallucinate and they sometimes return malformed JSON. “So we used the same System One principles [as Jev/Clef] there, and decided on extraction.” Some examples of system one use cases at Cloudflare. She used the example of an invoice, where an LLM will sometimes get an important detail wrong — like the order number. “When you send it [the order] to an LLM, they're like, wait, I think the order number's three, maybe it's four, maybe it's five. But it's like, the number's right there, you just have to read it! ” So the idea with Clairic is that it will extract a typed value — like a number — from unstructured data, in one forward pass. Using the label “neolab” sounds a bit like a marketing gimmick, but it also makes a ton of sense for Cloudflare to produce system one models — and even, in future, reasoning models. “Being a neolab means that we can create what we are missing,” Chen said in her presentation. In our interview, she also mentioned that creating their own models allows Cloudflare to derisk its AI operations. “I think there's a lot of risk in the AI space , because just like Jev was closed source and we couldn't run it, there [are] a lot of models out there [with] maybe regulatory risks coming up, like the Chinese open source models. I think lots of model labs want to actually make money, as well — so enforcing quite expensive licenses.” If you look at Cloudflare’s product page now, it resembles what Amazon’s cloud computing product page looked like at the height of Web 2.0 — i.e. there’s a lot there! But there’s still room for several more models.

item.title: Anthropic Adds Code Mode to Claude Code: Claude Now Chains Tool Calls in JavaScript
item.abstract: Anthropic has added Code Mode to Claude Code as an experimental, opt-in feature. Claude Code Code Mode is a mode in which Claude writes JavaScript that makes several tool calls in 1 step. It shipped in Claude Code v2.1.323 last week . For developers, it changes how the agent spends round-trips on multi-step work. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . Without Code Mode, Claude requests each Bash, Read or Edit call directly. It reads every result before choosing the next step. With Code Mode, Claude writes a piece of JavaScript, and Claude Code runs it in your session. According to the docs , one piece of code can run commands in parallel. It can feed one result into the next call. It can also return only the output Claude needs to read. Anthropic’s example raises a retry limit. The code finds the file, edits it and runs the tests: In the conversation, you see the tool calls, such as the diff. You do not see the code by default. Press Ctrl+O to open the transcript viewer and expand a collapsed Code row. Set CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_CODE_MODE=1 in your shell, or in the env block of ~/.claude/settings.json . Before the first session, Claude Code asks you to confirm. Select “Yes, turn on Code Mode”. Claude Code then restarts and shows ‘Code Mode (experimental) is on’. A Code Mode session resumes only with the variable still set to 1. Setting 0 anywhere turns it off, even if 1 is set elsewhere. Admins can block it org-wide with a 0 in managed settings . They cannot force it on. Anthropic recommends it for tasks with many related tool calls: Each tool call inside the code still passes your deny and ask rules. It also passes PreToolUse hooks under the tool’s usual name, such as Bash. Review differs by permission mode: Hook authors should check each part of a command. A git push can arrive as cd 'app' && git push . To inspect the code itself, match the REPL tool and read tool_input.code . If Claude waits, the code stops after 10 minutes, including time at permission prompts. In the background, it can run for up to 2 hours while you keep chatting. Background runs need a session started in auto or bypassPermissions mode. Cloudflare coined ‘Code Mode’ on September 26, 2025 . Its Agents SDK turns MCP schemas into a TypeScript API that runs in V8 isolates. Anthropic then published code execution with MCP . In one example, token use fell from 150,000 to 2,000, a 98.7% saving. Its API feature, Programmatic Tool Calling , uses Python. It cut average usage from 43,588 to 27,297 tokens on complex research tasks. Claude Code’s version applies the pattern to the CLI’s own tools. The docs give no token figure. One independent test reported system-tool context of 11.1k tokens with Code Mode versus 24.6k without. Treat that as a single third-party measurement. Check out the Code Mode documentation and the Claude Code changelog . You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension .
